platform_risks.fallback: Bid unrestricted commercial/municipal contracts without set-aside caps, or team exclusively with 'similarly situated entities' under 13 CFR § 125.6

chapters.subtitle: SAM.gov and Municipal Bid Desks: Earned Service Fees, Lawful Prime/Sub Teaming, Procurement Integrity, and FAR Operating Mechanics
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #4, Government Contract Brokering, holds Rank #27 of 29 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: a High-Leverage Operator Play, not an award-flipping shortcut. The operator sells procurement intelligence, bid production, supplier coordination, and documented contract administration while clients retain their contract obligations. Seven mapped plays organize the work: public_record_api_intelligence, solicitation triage, bid-calendar operations, proposal production, supplier qualification, prime/sub teaming coordination, and post-award administration. Recognized service fees, not client contract ceilings or purchases, drive the scorecard. Conservative, Base, and Scaled annual owner profit equals $18,000, $126,000, and $300,000 respectively. Durability comes from narrow category expertise, verified performance evidence, repeatable deliverables, and collection discipline; contingent-fee exposure, unsupported pass-through structures, and supplier failure destroy the model.

sections.heading: 1. Define the Paid Work Before Calling Yourself a Broker
paragraphs: Government contract brokering is a commercial shorthand, not a federal procurement license or a transferable right to an agency award. In this chapter, it means operating a specialist service business that helps qualified suppliers find solicitations, evaluate fit, assemble responses, coordinate legitimate teaming, and administer documented obligations. The customer usually is the supplier or prime contractor; the agency remains that customer's buyer. The service firm earns agreed fees for work performed rather than claiming the face value of contracts it touches. A $2 million municipal equipment award supported by a $12,000 proposal engagement produces at most $12,000 of service consideration for this operator, subject to performance and the applicable accounting treatment. It does not create $2 million of operator sales. If the firm instead signs as prime, controls promised goods or services, and carries delivery responsibility, it has entered a different contracting model requiring a separate principal-versus-agent assessment. Do not combine that model with this volume's service-fee scorecard. Begin each engagement by naming the contracting parties, deliverables, payment obligations, submission authority, and responsibility for every factual representation. Those boundaries determine what can be sold repeatedly without transferring unpriced delivery risk into a small bid desk.

The market supports five useful operator archetypes: intelligence desk, proposal studio, supplier qualification desk, teaming coordinator, and post-award administrator. Choose one initial buyer and one procurement category rather than advertising access to every government purchaser. A janitorial contractor needs wage-determination analysis, site-visit tracking, staffing evidence, and realistic mobilization assumptions; a distributor needs exact product equivalence, authorized sourcing, lead-time verification, and shipping terms. Those are different production systems. SAM.gov registration is generally the prospective federal contractor's responsibility under applicable requirements, and registration itself is free. Charge for documented preparation and maintenance work only when the customer understands that distinction. For municipal opportunities, verify the issuing jurisdiction's vendor registration, lobbying, disclosure, and procurement rules rather than copying federal clauses into every checklist. A durable engagement specifies monthly research coverage, a maximum number of evaluated opportunities, proposal complexity bands, response times, and exclusions. It also names who approves pricing and who signs certifications. A broker who uploads a proposal using somebody else's credentials has not created efficiency; they have obscured accountability. Use authorized portal roles where available and retain written submission instructions with the final package. Keep the customer's own designated signer responsible for representations and commitments.

Lawful fee design starts before lead generation. FAR Subpart 3.4 and FAR 52.203-5 address contingent fees for obtaining federal contracts, with defined treatment for bona fide employees and established commercial or selling agencies. The exceptions are fact-dependent, not a label that any consultant can adopt. Prefer scoped retainers and fixed deliverable fees, while reviewing the actual arrangement and applicable solicitation terms; changing an invoice description does not cure improper influence. Procurement integrity restrictions under 41 U.S.C. 2102 and FAR 3.104 prohibit specified conduct involving contractor bid or proposal information and source-selection information before award. The Anti-Kickback Act separately addresses improper payments connected with favorable treatment under federal prime contracts and subcontracts. A referral payment to a prime's employee is therefore not equivalent to paying an independent researcher for documented work. Set-aside eligibility, limitations on subcontracting, organizational conflicts, and applicable excessive pass-through charge clauses can defeat otherwise attractive structures. Map each rule to the actual transaction instead of describing all teaming as prohibited. Your product is a reliable operating process, not agency influence. Never imply that a personal relationship can override competition, responsibility findings, evaluation criteria, or the contracting officer's authority.

callout.title: Verify the Transaction Before Accepting the Engagement
callout.body: Document these four checks in the engagement file before proposing a fee or contacting potential partners.
items: Identify the paying customer, authorized signer, actual contractor, and every promised deliverable; separate advisory work from prime performance.
Review contingent-fee terms, referral compensation, procurement integrity exposure, and applicable agency or municipal restrictions against the actual facts.

Confirm portal permissions, certification ownership, supplier evidence access, and the customer's ability to fund the agreed service fees.

sections.heading: 2. Map Seven Plays Into a Narrow, Defensible Bid Desk
paragraphs: Seven plays fit this business. The supplied mapped identifier is public_record_api_intelligence; the other six labels here describe chapter-specific operating workstreams rather than additional registry identifiers. Public-record intelligence converts lawful public signals into qualified supplier conversations and procurement forecasts. County dockets, probate registries, unclaimed property ledgers, and public APIs can reveal ownership transitions, unresolved administrative work, or business events, but none automatically proves a procurement need or an uncontested claim. Connect each signal to an identifiable service requirement, purchasing authority, and legitimate customer. For government sales, budget hearings, capital plans, expiring awards, and agency procurement forecasts usually provide more direct evidence. An illustrative batch of 400 records yielding 40 relevant events, eight supplier conversations, and one $2,000 monthly engagement creates $24,000 of annual fees only if twelve months of service are delivered. It creates no revenue merely because a lead exists. Record source URLs, retrieval dates, permitted use, and confidence levels. If APIs fail or access terms change, switch to scheduled bulk FOIA or state public-record exports, official data feeds, and low-frequency cached queues. FOIA processing time and exemptions make it a research channel, not a dependable last-minute bid feed.

Solicitation triage, bid-calendar operations, and proposal production turn signals into bounded work. For triage, screen 120 notices monthly against geography, NAICS alignment, capacity, incumbent evidence, and mandatory qualifications; twelve credible matches and four customer-authorized pursuits are a better output than 120 forwarded emails. At an illustrative $2,000 monthly service price, the unit is qualified coverage, not a promised award. Bid-calendar operations track questions, amendments, site visits, bonding, quote validity, and submission timestamps. Twenty live pursuits requiring fifteen minutes of weekly maintenance consume five hours before exception handling. Price that workload inside the retainer and reduce coverage when amendment volume exceeds capacity. Proposal production can sell an $8,000 package with forty planned production hours, equivalent to $200 per planned hour before overhead and rework. Separate technical writing, cost inputs, attachments, and final assembly so customer delays remain visible. The fallback for a missing mandatory credential is a documented no-bid decision, not creative wording. The fallback for an overloaded production queue is a narrower pursuit count or a vetted specialist under a bounded assignment. These plays strengthen one another only when they share a single opportunity record and explicit customer decisions about what deserves expensive production time.

Supplier qualification, prime/sub teaming coordination, and post-award administration complete the seven-play map. A $4,000 qualification package covering eight suppliers budgets $500 per supplier before shared overhead; verify capability, required representations, capacity, source authenticity, exclusions, and references rather than collecting attractive brochures. If no supplier meets the requirements, deliver the documented finding and stop the pursuit. A $5,000 teaming coordination milestone requiring twenty-five hours yields $200 per planned hour before expenses; define scope allocation, pricing dependencies, confidentiality, and negotiation ownership without promising award. If the proposed prime lacks required eligibility or cannot perform its required share, restructure lawfully or abandon the arrangement. Post-award administration at $3,000 monthly for fifteen planned hours likewise starts at $200 per planned hour, but disputed acceptance can erase that capacity quickly. Bound invoice support, deliverable tracking, and modification logs; leave changes to authorized contract personnel. Use named portals as workflow infrastructure, not as substitutes for category knowledge. The comparison matrix shows sixteen distinct entry points. Its prices are illustrative service packages, not published platform rates or incremental revenue to add automatically to the scorecard. Select a lane where repeated specifications and recurring buyers let evidence compound across engagements without copying confidential client material into another customer's proposal.

callout.title: Build Evidence That Survives the Next Solicitation
callout.body: Experienced bid desks preserve decision quality rather than maximizing the number of proposals submitted.
items: Save the original solicitation, every amendment, and retrieval timestamps; compare changed requirements before reusing an earlier response matrix.
Read incumbent award history through SAM.gov and USAspending.gov, but distinguish ceilings, obligations, modifications, and actual competitive scope.
Set supplier quote expiration several days beyond the planned customer decision date; obtain refreshed written commitments before final pricing.
Record why each pursuit was rejected, then tune alerts around recurring disqualifiers instead of buying progressively larger notice feeds.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile Earned Fees, Cash Timing, and the Three Profit Cases
paragraphs: Use an earned-fee ledger that separates contracted consideration, cash collected, services performed, recognized revenue, and remaining obligations. Signing a twelve-month $24,000 engagement does not automatically create $24,000 of current revenue. A monthly stand-ready service may be recognized over its service period when the applicable accounting criteria are met; a discrete proposal package follows the actual performance obligation and transfer of control. Customer acceptance provisions matter when substantive, but an invoice date alone does not establish performance. An advance for future work generally remains a liability until earned. Track service credits, refund rights, disputes, and variable consideration rather than assuming every invoice becomes permanent revenue. Keep client award values in a separate operational field so dashboards cannot quietly convert procurement volume into service sales. A $10 million indefinite-delivery contract ceiling also differs from obligated orders and from a supplier's realized revenue. None is this operator's recognized revenue merely because the bid desk helped prepare the submission. Establish these definitions in the chart of accounts and reporting specification before building automation. That discipline prevents a visually impressive pipeline from concealing weak collections, unfinished engagements, and fees that remain subject to valid customer credits or contractual refunds.

The canonical Conservative case is $120,000 annual gross service revenue, a 15% net margin, and $18,000 annual owner net profit with two full-time people and three contractors. One illustrative earned-fee bridge is four clients at $2,000 monthly for twelve months, producing $96,000, plus six completed $4,000 packages, producing $24,000. Total modeled costs must therefore equal $102,000. The Base case is $560,000 revenue, a 22.5% margin, and $126,000 profit with the same roster: eight clients at $4,000 monthly produce $384,000, and twenty-two $8,000 packages produce $176,000. Costs equal $434,000. The Scaled case uses three full-time people and four contractors: ten clients at $6,000 monthly produce $720,000, while twenty-eight $10,000 packages produce $280,000. Revenue reaches $1,000,000, costs equal $700,000, and the 30% margin yields $300,000 owner profit. These bridges assume full-year delivery and distinct package work outside retainer scope; they are not acquisition forecasts. Contractor counts describe available people rather than full-time-equivalent utilization. The Conservative cost envelope is particularly tight for two full-time roles. Validate actual compensation and overhead before treating that roster as affordable, and preserve the canonical scenario separately from any local staffing revision.

Startup capital of $20,000 to $90,000 and a six-to-eighteen-month time to first deal demand deliberate runway planning. The stated $5,000 to $25,000 monthly operating-expense range must not be confused with an all-inclusive cap on annual scenario costs. Base and Scaled total costs average approximately $36,167 and $58,333 monthly respectively, including whatever delivery costs the model requires. If the stated operating range is interpreted as fully inclusive, that interpretation conflicts with the canonical totals; keep the distinction visible instead of forcing a false reconciliation. At $5,000 monthly burn, $25,000 provides five months before setup costs, shorter than the earliest stated deal timing. At $25,000 monthly burn, even $150,000 supplies only six months before setup costs. Build a weekly cash schedule and sell paid readiness work where useful, rather than funding all effort until an award. Federal prompt-payment provisions do not automatically make the service firm's supplier customer pay on the agency's timetable. Specify deposits, earned milestones, invoice disputes, and suspension rights. Under stress, pause unfunded work, reduce pursuit counts, and revalidate collections before hiring. Award uncertainty, payment delays, and supplier failure are separate exposures and require separate reserves, contract terms, and operating responses.

sections.heading: 4. Build a Small-Team Moat With Evidence, Permissions, and Controlled Workload
paragraphs: A durable small-team moat is the accumulated ability to reject bad pursuits quickly and deliver good ones without reconstructing every fact. Start with a customer-owned evidence library containing approved capability statements, past-performance references, licenses, resumes, insurance evidence, and sourcing documentation. Tag each artifact with its owner, expiration, permitted uses, and verification date. Store public research separately from confidential client materials. Microsoft SharePoint can manage controlled documents, while a carefully permissioned Airtable base or PostgreSQL database can track opportunities and deadlines. Tool selection matters less than access separation, backups, and a reliable amendment process. Use SAM.gov alerts and official feeds for discovery, calendar automation for dates, and checklists for recurring requirements; do not automate factual certifications or assume generated text accurately describes customer capabilities. Require source evidence for every material claim. An analyst can prepare a draft, a specialist can review technical fit, and the customer's authorized signer can approve commitments. For controlled information, use only environments and handling procedures permitted by the relevant requirements. A generic shared workspace does not satisfy every contract's security obligations. When requirements exceed the desk's supported environment, narrow the engagement to permissible material or decline that portion.

Operational discipline begins with an explicit bid/no-bid record. Capture mandatory eligibility, delivery capacity, credible pricing inputs, submission feasibility, and customer funding before assigning writing hours. A scored pursuit sheet should support judgment, not manufacture precision from weak assumptions. Track qualified opportunities, authorized pursuits, submitted responses, awards, earned fees, overdue receivables, rework hours, and customer concentration as separate measures. An award rate can improve while owner profit deteriorates if the desk accepts increasingly complex packages at unchanged fees. Likewise, a low award rate can coexist with useful, well-delivered research services, but persistent customer losses usually damage retention. Review both outcomes and contracted service quality. Protect procurement integrity by prohibiting solicitation of protected competitor information and recording the source of unusual market intelligence. Check organizational conflicts under FAR Subpart 9.5 when the desk's roles could create biased ground rules, impaired objectivity, or unequal access to information. Do not advise competing clients on the same live procurement without addressing confidentiality, contractual restrictions, and actual conflicts. If a customer requests an unsupported certification, stop that submission path and resolve the evidence gap. False statements and claims can create exposure far beyond the value of a proposal fee.

Launch with a ninety-day evidence-building cycle rather than a promise to close an award within ninety days. During the first month, select one category, interview qualified suppliers, review recent solicitations, and test a paid readiness package. During the second month, run the full workflow on a small number of authorized pursuits and measure actual production hours, customer input delays, amendment volume, and correction rates. During the third month, adjust scope and pricing from those observations, then decide whether recurring coverage has enough demand to justify another hire. Preserve the stated six-to-eighteen-month first-deal horizon when planning contract-award-dependent activity. Require a supplier contingency plan before submission: alternate sources must satisfy the solicitation, preserve quote validity, and remain consistent with the offered technical solution. After award, route changes through the authorized contractual process instead of letting informal buyer requests expand the client's obligations. Close each engagement with evidence of delivered services, billing reconciliation, lessons learned, and the next renewal decision. The strongest desk can explain exactly why a pursuit was selected, what it produced, what the customer approved, and how the resulting fee was earned. That audit trail is commercially valuable even when the agency selects another supplier.

The check usually comes from a contractor's operating account, not an agency procurement officer. sections.heading: 1. Sell to the Budget Owner Who Absorbs the Failure
paragraphs: Start by identifying the legal customer, the budget owner, and the person who can accept your work; they are often three different parties. A small prime's president may want more bids, their controller may control vendor payments, and their proposal manager may certify delivery. The government contracting officer normally pays the awarded contractor, not an outside adviser hired by that contractor. A contracting officer's representative may inspect performance without possessing authority to change price or obligate additional funds. Under FAR 1.602-1, contracting officers bind the government only within delegated authority. Therefore, a friendly agency introduction, purchase forecast, or program manager email cannot substitute for an authorized contract. For a private contractor engagement, obtain the customer's executed service order, purchasing authorization, billing address, and accounts-payable contact before starting. For a direct municipal engagement, inspect the actual charter, purchasing ordinance, appropriation, and delegation documents rather than transplanting federal rules. Separate signature authority from banking authority: the person requesting a supplier setup form may have neither. Your first sales deliverable is a one-page authority map connecting the buyer's operational problem to an enforceable payment obligation and a named acceptance owner.

The strongest buyer is paying to remove a measurable bottleneck, not to purchase influence over an award. A proposal director sees an approaching deadline and insufficient reviewer capacity; a CFO sees delivered work trapped behind rejected invoices; a supplier manager sees a subcontractor whose missing records threaten the prime's performance. Translate each problem into controllable service units. A $5,000 bid package might include a solicitation crosswalk, amendment log, pricing workbook checks, and submission evidence, while leaving technical certifications with the customer. If it replaces 40 internal hours budgeted at $150 each, the comparison is $6,000 of internal capacity against a $5,000 external fee, not a promised contract win. Similarly, a $2,500 acceptance-evidence package can be evaluated against the customer's documented rework hours and collection delay. Do not claim that assembling documents creates statutory eligibility or compels an agency to pay. Ask buyers which rejected document, missed amendment, or unresolved discrepancy caused their last loss. Their answer reveals the acceptance test they will actually fund. Procurement anxiety supports a sale only when your scope converts that anxiety into specific work, bounded responsibility, and inspectable evidence that another employee can verify.

Use seven chapter-level commercial mappings: capture retainers, bid packages, supplier onboarding, acceptance evidence, municipal readiness, teaming administration, and sponsored directory placements. These are service offers, not seven permissions to intermediate public money. A $4,000 monthly capture retainer buys monitored opportunities and a maintained bid calendar; a $3,000 teaming assignment buys documented workshare and responsibility coordination, not an award-dependent introduction. The directory offer is the specified ego_bait_directory_badge_arbitrage play, monetized through advertising sold separately from rankings. Each offer needs its own payer and deliverable because the advertising buyer may have no procurement relationship with any listed agency. For federal opportunities, screen contingent compensation against FAR Subpart 3.4 and applicable FAR 52.203-5 terms; bona fide employee and established commercial or selling agency exceptions require actual factual support. Renaming a success fee as consulting does not change its substance. Fixed fees also do not sanitize improper influence, kickbacks, or misuse of protected information. When the customer insists on paying only after an award, offer a smaller prepaid diagnostic or decline that compensation structure. Preserve a commercially useful service relationship without making the public procurement decision your payment trigger.

callout.body: Experienced bid desks qualify the payer as carefully as the solicitation. These tactics expose collection problems before they become unpaid labor.
items: Ask for a redacted rejected invoice or missed-amendment example; build the scope around the actual failure rather than a generic promise of more awards.
Have the customer's accounts-payable team confirm the purchase-order reference, invoice channel, and vendor setup before the proposal team receives production work.
Maintain SAM.gov opportunity identifiers and amendment timestamps in the delivery record; preserve the customer's final submission receipt separately.
Give directory winners a free branded badge regardless of advertising purchases; retain dated ranking inputs so sales staff cannot rewrite the result.

sections.heading: 2. Separate the Service Invoice from the Government Disbursement
paragraphs: Draw two money paths before selecting a payment method. The agency-to-prime path follows the public contract, acceptance requirements, proper-invoice rules, and designated disbursement system. The prime-to-adviser path follows your separate service agreement unless you are directly contracted by the agency. A $2 million government award remains the contractor's contract value; a $5,000 bid-desk invoice is your service revenue when earned under the applicable accounting policy. Never route the full award through your account merely to extract a fee. Federal electronic payments generally operate under 31 CFR Part 208, while the applicable contract may use FAR 52.232-33 and banking information maintained through SAM.gov. Invoice submission still depends on the agency and contract: Treasury's Invoice Processing Platform and DoD's Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment are examples, not interchangeable destinations. Municipal systems have their own vendor registration and remittance instructions. Map the purchase order, invoice identifier, receiving record, and remittance reference so the controller can reconcile each payment without guessing. A remittance notice is not bank settlement, and bank settlement does not establish that your performance obligations are complete. Track invoiced, accepted, paid, and earned amounts as separate fields.

The eight commonly proposed rails combine actual transfer methods with commercial arrangements, so compare them on custody, finality, and release authority rather than calling them equivalent. A wire can move a deposit quickly but provides no automatic dispute adjudication. ACH is usually efficient for recurring business payments, but return exposure depends on transaction type, authorization, timing, and applicable rules. Escrow introduces an independent holder and a written release mechanism; it does not manufacture an agency appropriation or override contractual assignment restrictions. Retainers and milestone holds define when money is due, while an underlying wire, ACH transfer, or card transaction moves it. For example, split a $5,000 bid package into a $2,500 deposit and $2,500 payable upon documented delivery. If the customer needs a holdback, cap it at an agreed amount tied to an explicit checklist instead of waiting indefinitely for an award. A platform checkout through Stripe or Square can simplify a $500 directory subscription, but card disputes remain possible. Disclose renewal terms, retain placement evidence, and provide a clear cancellation process. The checkout receipt should identify advertising services, not imply that the buyer purchased public certification or preferred access to government decision-makers.

Public payment timing requires contract-specific analysis. The Prompt Payment Act, including 31 U.S.C. 3903, and 5 CFR Part 1315 establish federal payment requirements and interest mechanisms; they do not make every private service invoice payable on a universal schedule. FAR 52.232-25, when applicable, links payment administration to proper invoices and acceptance conditions. FAR 52.232-40 addresses accelerated payments to small business subcontractors without creating a new Prompt Payment Act entitlement or automatically rewriting the subcontract's payment terms. If a prime offers factoring as your collection solution, identify whose receivable is being sold. An assignment of federal contract proceeds may implicate 31 U.S.C. 3727, 41 U.S.C. 6305, and FAR Subpart 32.8; ordinary broker instructions cannot replace those requirements. Financing also introduces fees, reserves, recourse, and dilution risk. On an illustrative $50,000 eligible receivable, an 85% advance supplies $42,500, leaving $7,500 before reserves and charges. That advance is liquidity against the receivable, not new service revenue. When eligibility or assignment is disputed, use a smaller prepaid service scope rather than assuming a financier will cure weak documentation or an unenforceable payment claim.

sections.heading: 3. Protect Fees with Evidence, Credit Limits, and Lawful Workshare
paragraphs: Fee protection begins with scope architecture, not an intimidating noncircumvention paragraph. Define the customer entities covered, named deliverables, customer dependencies, permitted use, price, acceptance criteria, change procedure, and collection terms. A bid-package engagement can require written identification of missing checklist items within five business days, followed by a specified correction process; the enforceability and effect of silence must be checked under the governing agreement and applicable law. Preserve version history in SharePoint or a controlled document repository, plus delivery receipts and the customer's requested changes. Tie the final invoice to delivery of the contracted service, not the government's award decision. Use a narrowly defined confidentiality and work-product license arrangement to protect research, templates, and authorized introductions without restricting lawful public competition. Any noncircumvention provision needs a defined relationship, duration, and legitimate scope; it cannot confer ownership of a publicly posted solicitation. Avoid percentage tails on government awards disguised as protection against bypass. If the prime brings the work in-house, collect for completed milestones and the expressly purchased capacity, subject to the agreement, rather than claiming an unearned slice of future public spending. This turns a potentially emotional bypass dispute into a narrower evidentiary collection problem.

Credit-screen the actual payer before extending terms. Confirm legal existence through the relevant secretary of state, match the contracting entity to its tax and payment records, and inspect exclusions where relevant through SAM.gov. Active registration is not evidence of solvency. USAspending.gov can help test claims about federal award history, but obligations and reported awards are not available cash. Request recent receivables aging, customer concentration, references from comparable service vendors, and evidence of the authorized purchasing process. Review public liens, litigation, and bankruptcy records through appropriate official systems and PACER where useful; interpret findings with the entity and jurisdiction correctly matched. Establish exposure limits in dollars. For a new $5,000 package, a $2,500 deposit limits the unpaid contract balance to $2,500 before approved changes. A $4,000 retainer billed after service can become $8,000 of receivables when a second month begins unpaid, with additional unbilled work increasing exposure. Stop new discretionary work at the contractual threshold and notify the customer before suspension. For essential existing obligations, follow the agreed termination and transition provisions rather than abruptly withholding files the customer already owns. Credit policy should protect cash without creating a fresh performance breach.

Lawful teaming requires an actual performance role. Under FAR 9.6, contractor team arrangements can organize complementary capabilities, but the label does not excuse a shell prime that contributes no meaningful value. FAR 52.215-22 and 52.215-23 address excessive pass-through charges when applicable; check their inclusion and the transaction facts rather than asserting a universal prohibition on subcontracting. Small-business set-asides add distinct requirements under 13 CFR 125.6 and, where incorporated, FAR 52.219-14. For covered services, the general limitation concerns amounts paid to firms that are not similarly situated, with contract-category rules and specified exclusions requiring careful calculation. Review affiliation and ostensible subcontractor issues under 13 CFR 121.103 as well. Procurement integrity restrictions in 41 U.S.C. 2102 protect contractor bid or proposal information and source-selection information before award. Anti-kickback restrictions in 41 U.S.C. 8702 reach improper benefits used to obtain or reward favorable treatment in covered contracting. Never pay a prime employee personally to route subcontract work, and never buy competitor proposal contents. The fallback is a documented service assignment with permitted information, real deliverables, and traceable payment to the contracting business. If the economics require hidden influence or fictitious workshare, abandon that structure before preparing the invoice.

sections.heading: 4. Reconcile Seven Service Plays to the Three Canonical Profit Cases
paragraphs: The scorecard recognizes service fees, not client award value, escrow balances, or factoring advances. Its Conservative case is $120,000 revenue at 15% net margin, leaving $18,000 annual owner net profit and $102,000 of modeled costs with 2 FT + 3 C. The Base case is $560,000 revenue at 22.5%, leaving $126,000 profit and $434,000 of modeled costs with the same team counts. Scaled is $1,000,000 revenue at 30%, leaving $300,000 profit and $700,000 of modeled costs with 3 FT + 4 C, seven people total. The table supplies one illustrative revenue mix that reconciles exactly to each case; it does not claim these prices or sales volumes are observed market results. Contractor counts do not specify hours, and the Conservative cost envelope must be tested against actual compensation before hiring. In particular, $102,000 cannot casually be treated as funding five full-time market-rate positions. Track delivery hours and contribution by offer so heavy proposal revisions do not consume the retainer margin. A $5,000 package requiring 40 hours yields $125 per delivery hour before overhead; at 80 hours that falls to $62.50. Use scope boundaries and priced change orders, not optimistic award probabilities, to protect those economics.

For ego_bait_directory_badge_arbitrage, publish data-scored state and city lists such as 'Top 15 Verified Specialists in Austin' using documented verification criteria. State precisely what verified means: for example, checked business identity and documented specialty evidence, not government endorsement or award eligibility. Issue free embeddable 'Top Rated' winner badges only to firms meeting the published method. Freeze each published edition's objective scores against commercial editing; retain the input snapshot and publish factual corrections transparently. Sell $299–$799 monthly Featured #1 Lead-Capture placements in a separate 'Sponsored / Featured' advertising area, never by rewriting the underlying ranking. At $500 monthly, three annual subscriptions produce $18,000, matching the Base bridge. Five specialists in each of 20 cities embedding a badge would produce 100 referring sites, but neither adoption nor domain-rating scores are assured. Earn hundreds of links through genuine distribution, not purchased ranking treatment. Use clean branded anchor text, distinguish sponsored links appropriately, and never promise search position. FTC Act Section 5 and applicable endorsement principles require truthful presentation of the commercial relationship. If badge adoption or lead quality disappoints, retain the free objective directory, stop unsupported performance claims, and let advertisers cancel rather than manipulating scores to rescue subscription revenue.

The other six plays need equally explicit fallbacks. Capture retainers sell a $4,000 monthly monitoring scope; reduce coverage or pause renewal when no useful opportunities fit. Bid packages sell $5,000 deliverables; collect for accepted work when a customer abandons a bid. Supplier onboarding sells $2,000 files; record unresolved evidence instead of inventing eligibility. Acceptance packages sell $2,500 documentation assignments; escalate disputes without representing that the agency must release cash. Municipal readiness sells $7,500 jurisdiction-specific projects; narrow scope when local requirements expand. Teaming administration sells $3,000 assignments; stop when proposed workshare or compensation cannot survive the applicable rules. These controls address award uncertainty, payment delays, and supplier failure without merging the operator's receivable with the client's public contract. The stated $20,000–$90,000 startup range and $5,000–$25,000 monthly opex range do not establish sufficient runway for a 6–18 month first-deal cycle. At $25,000 monthly, $150,000 covers six months before setup costs; eighteen months would consume $450,000. Treat the opex range as a planning input, not a replacement for the scenario's complete cost reconciliation. Launch with paid diagnostics, committed deposits, and flexible contractor hours, and forecast cash weekly. Automate solicitation alerts, bid calendars, and checklist reminders while retaining human review of authority, certifications, and payment exceptions.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #4, Government Contract Brokering, ranks #27 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Its economics depend on recognized service fees, not the face value of contracts sourced through SAM.gov or municipal portals. This chapter develops seven mapped plays as operating variants of the supplied brokerage play: federal sourcing, municipal sourcing, janitorial coordination, grounds coordination, courier coordination, translation coordination, and IT staffing coordination. Canonical annual owner profit is $18,000 Conservative, $126,000 Base, and $300,000 Scaled. The waterfall separates scope credits from delivery labor, customer acquisition, operating overhead, and collection losses. Working-capital tests expose acceptance holds and invoice delays before they consume contractor payroll. Fixed deliverable fees, documented management work, and lawful teaming structures make the spread defensible; an award announcement alone creates neither earned revenue nor spendable cash.

sections.heading: 1. Define the fee-bearing unit before calculating a management spread
paragraphs: Start with the signed service agreement, not the solicitation's estimated ceiling. The canonical revenue basis is recognized service fees, excluding client contract value, subcontractor pass-through principal, and unexercised options. The supplied mapped play, government_rfp_subcontractor_brokerage, uses SAM.gov, state procurement portals, and municipal bid boards to locate low-bid-density service opportunities and coordinate qualified fulfillment. Its advertised 15–30% management spread is an underwriting range, not an automatic accounting treatment. On a $100,000 client service package, $80,000 of supplier delivery and $20,000 of separately earned desk fees produce a 20% fee share of package value and a 25% markup on supplier cost. Those percentages answer different questions. If the desk instead contracts as principal and controls the promised service, gross presentation may be required; a $20,000 margin cannot simply be relabeled $20,000 of revenue. Keep that principal model outside this fee-based scorecard until the accounting policy and scenario are rebuilt. Maintain a deal record linking the customer, solicitation identifier, fee payer, delivery obligations, acceptance evidence, supplier invoices, and recognized fee. A purchase order ceiling is pipeline capacity; only satisfied contractual performance supports the operating revenue ledger.

For this chapter, seven mapped plays mean seven operating variants of that single supplied catalog identifier, not seven invented catalog entries. Federal sourcing and municipal sourcing monetize bid-desk deliverables; janitorial, grounds, courier, translation, and IT staffing coordination monetize distinct management work. Price sourcing through fixed retainers or completed milestones where appropriate, rather than assuming an award percentage is permissible. FAR Subpart 3.4 and FAR 52.203-5 restrict contingent-fee arrangements within their applicable scope; the bona fide employee or agency exception requires factual qualification, not a label in an invoice. Likewise, 41 U.S.C. 2102 protects specified procurement information, and 41 U.S.C. 8702 prohibits kickbacks connected with covered prime contracts and subcontracts. No pricing model should require buying source-selection information or paying an undisclosed reward for favorable treatment. A percentage can illustrate coordination economics without authorizing a commission for obtaining an award. State and municipal requirements must be checked separately. Record the actual service, fee trigger, customer benefit, and applicable restrictions before a salesperson promises a spread. The matrix shows illustrative standalone units; its rows are alternative delivery motions, not additive components of the canonical annual revenue totals.

Screen structure before calculating contribution. For covered small-business service contracts, 13 CFR 125.6 generally limits payments to subcontractors that are not similarly situated to 50% of the amount paid by the government for contract performance, subject to the rule's definitions and exclusions. A similarly situated entity must meet the relevant program status and size requirements; location alone proves nothing. Further subcontracting can affect the limitation calculation, and ostensible-subcontractor concerns remain a separate affiliation issue. A broker retaining 20% while sending 80% to an ineligible fulfillment company can therefore have attractive arithmetic and an unusable structure. Check FAR 52.215-23 when applicable: a pass-through charge needs substantive added value, not merely invoice routing. The fallback is an unrestricted opportunity whose actual terms permit the structure, including suitable commercial or municipal work, or a properly qualified similarly situated team. Municipal status does not erase local subcontracting restrictions. Document scheduling, quality inspection, customer reporting, replacement coverage, and dispute resolution as management deliverables. If those services cannot justify the fee, sell a narrower fixed-price bid-desk engagement instead. Reject a tempting award when eligibility, delivery control, or fee legality cannot support the proposed economics.

callout.title: Verify the structure before pricing the fee
callout.body: The spreadsheet becomes actionable only after the contracting structure, recognition basis, performance obligations, and cash obligations agree.
items: Identify whether the desk is service provider, agent, subcontractor, or prime; document why the scorecard includes only its recognized fees.
Check the solicitation and agreement against FAR contingent-fee provisions, procurement-integrity restrictions, and applicable state or municipal requirements.
For a covered set-aside, calculate the 13 CFR 125.6 limitation using actual supplier status and further-subcontracting facts.
Obtain executable supplier pricing, acceptance criteria, replacement coverage, and payment terms before committing customer delivery dates.

sections.heading: 2. Reconcile annual cohorts from gross fee billings to owner profit
paragraphs: Use an annual cohort of completed fee-bearing engagements to reconcile the three canonical scenarios. The illustrative customer counts are six Conservative, fourteen Base, and twenty Scaled, producing average recognized annual fees of $20,000, $40,000, and $50,000 per customer. Gross earned fee billings before scope credits are $126,000, $580,000, and $1,040,000. Expected contractual credits and performance reversals of $6,000, $20,000, and $40,000 reduce those amounts to exactly $120,000, $560,000, and $1,000,000 of recognized service revenue. This is a steady-state annual cohort illustration: no opening deferred balances or unfinished performance are embedded in the bridge. In a live ledger, reconcile invoicing, earned amounts, contract liabilities, and unbilled receivables separately. The credit assumptions equal 4.76%, 3.45%, and 3.85% of gross fee billings, respectively. They represent fee reductions for narrowed scope, rejected deliverables, or documented service failures; they are not interchangeable with losses on valid receivables. Exclude unawarded pipeline entirely. A bid lost before contracted work is earned creates acquisition expense or idle capacity, not a reversal of imaginary award revenue. Each cohort must reconcile to signed fee schedules and actual performance before its margin is used for hiring.

Delivery labor is $54,000, $252,000, and $420,000 across the cases. An explicit staffing assumption makes the low case intelligible: its two full-time people are a working owner taking residual profit and one employee budgeted at $36,000 fully loaded, plus three contractors sharing $18,000 of delivery invoices. That employee budget requires location-specific wage and benefit validation and may be inadequate. The Base case assumes $72,000 for the paid employee and $180,000 across three contractors; the Scaled case assumes two paid employees at $90,000 each and $240,000 across four contractors, alongside the working owner. Contractor counts describe a delivery bench, not full-time-equivalent salaries. Acquisition spending of $12,000, $56,000, and $80,000 yields customer acquisition costs of $2,000, $4,000, and $4,000 using the cohort counts above. Include unsuccessful proposal work in that spending and do not also charge those hours to delivery. After labor and acquisition, contribution is $54,000, $252,000, and $500,000. Named software such as Microsoft 365, Airtable, and QuickBooks belongs in the platform budget, not hidden inside a fictional zero-cost automation assumption. Separate proposal production time, customer management time, and supplier fulfillment time in weekly timesheets.

The remaining deductions are platform, insurance, and operating support of $18,000, $70,000, and $110,000; financing, collection losses, and payment administration of $3,000, $14,000, and $20,000; and fixed administrative overhead of $15,000, $42,000, and $70,000. Total expenses therefore equal $102,000, $434,000, and $700,000, leaving the exact canonical owner profits of $18,000, $126,000, and $300,000. No additional market-rate owner salary is deducted in this illustration; residual profit compensates ownership and the owner's full-time labor before personal taxes. The Conservative case is consequently a fragile owner-operated business, not evidence that five people receive comfortable full-time compensation. Split the combined financing line internally: Conservative budgets $1,000 each for financing, collection losses, and payment administration; Base budgets $8,000, $4,000, and $2,000; Scaled budgets $10,000, $6,000, and $4,000. Collection losses remain an expense against otherwise valid receivables, while contractual fee credits stay above recognized revenue. Reserve releases must follow resolved evidence rather than a target margin. Reconcile gross profit, contribution, and owner profit as distinct subtotals so a strong supplier spread cannot conceal an expensive bid desk.

sections.heading: 3. Fund acceptance holds and invoice DSO without borrowing against fiction
paragraphs: Measure the cash clock from the first delivery outlay, not from the award notice. Separate mobilization before performance, acceptance or milestone-release holds before invoicing, invoice-to-cash days sales outstanding, and supplier payment dates. The illustration assumes immediate operating outlays, no supplier credit, and a fifteen-day pre-invoice acceptance hold in every case. Invoice DSO is thirty, sixty, and seventy-five days, producing cash gaps of forty-five, seventy-five, and ninety days. These are planning assumptions, not statutory payment promises. If the desk invoices a prime rather than an agency, the relevant collectible obligation is the prime's signed agreement with the desk. Federal prompt-payment provisions do not automatically turn every subcontract invoice into a direct government receivable. Check 31 U.S.C. 3903, FAR Subpart 32.9, and applicable payment clauses for the actual transaction. FAR 52.232-40 addresses accelerated payments to small-business subcontractors when its conditions apply, but it does not supply an unconditional accelerated cash date. For municipal work, obtain the jurisdiction's payment provisions and the customer's acceptance workflow. A missing purchase-order reference, incorrect remittance record, or disputed timesheet can extend collection even when the buyer has adequate appropriations.

Use total annual expense divided by 365 as a deliberately conservative daily funding proxy: approximately $279.45 Conservative, $1,189.04 Base, and $1,917.81 Scaled. This includes collection-loss allowances and other budgeted charges that may not be immediate cash payments, so it is a screening calculation rather than a substitute for a dated cash forecast. Multiplying by the assumed cash gaps gives approximately $12,575, $89,178, and $172,603 of operating float. Add thirty days of expense buffer, approximately $8,384, $35,671, and $57,534, producing rounded funding targets of $20,959, $124,849, and $230,137. Calculate totals before rounding the displayed components. The Scaled target exceeds the stated $20,000–$90,000 startup capital range; expansion therefore needs accumulated cash, contracted advances, suitable credit, or slower starts. The stated $5,000–$25,000 monthly operating range also cannot describe all-in spending at scale: canonical annual expenses imply approximately $8,500, $36,167, and $58,333 monthly. Keep the monthly range as an early-stage planning reference rather than silently forcing mature delivery expenses underneath it. Neither an unsigned credit proposal nor an anticipated award closes a funding gap.

Build a thirteen-week cash schedule by customer and weekly payment date. Enter earned invoices, expected acceptance dates, disputed amounts, supplier payroll deadlines, taxes, insurance renewals, and available credit. A fifteen-day hold belongs before invoice DSO here; if an actual arrangement instead withholds cash after collection, model that separate restriction without counting the same delay twice. The Base case's $124,849 target falls to $104,849 if two customers each provide an available $10,000 advance, but the advances remain contract liabilities until earned and must be restored if refund obligations arise. Confirm that their terms permit operational use. Supplier credit can reduce float only where enforceable terms support it; a contractor's informal willingness to wait is not financing. A thirty-day DSO extension adds approximately $8,384, $35,671, or $57,534 to required funding before incremental borrowing charges. Reserve a committed facility for that timing shock rather than using it to justify structurally negative contracts. Validate assignment restrictions, lender collateral terms, and any applicable federal assignment requirements before pledging receivables. Review actual bank availability weekly, because borrowing-base exclusions can remove disputed, aged, or concentrated invoices precisely when the desk needs liquidity most.

callout.title: Shorten the administrative cash gap before buying more leads
callout.body: Experienced bid desks collect evidence continuously and distinguish customer acceptance friction from actual funding scarcity.
items: Send a sample invoice and supporting-document checklist to the prime's accounts-payable team before the first delivery milestone.
Track acceptance aging separately from invoice aging so an apparently healthy DSO metric cannot hide unbilled completed work.
Negotiate smaller accepted milestones and supplier billing intervals rather than relying on an unpriced promise to wait for payment.
Keep customer advances, credit-loss allowances, contractual fee credits, and unrestricted operating cash in separate ledger accounts and forecast lines.

sop_steps.title: Map the contractual cash clock
sop_steps.action: Record first outlay, acceptance conditions, invoice eligibility, customer payment terms, and supplier due dates.
sop_steps.detail: Assign an accountable person to every acceptance document and distinguish agency payment from prime-to-desk payment.

sop_steps.title: Reconcile the weekly collection population
sop_steps.action: Match earned fees, issued invoices, contractual credits, receivable losses, and bank receipts by engagement identifier.
sop_steps.detail: Investigate invoice rejection reasons and unbilled completed milestones before changing the forecast collection date.

sop_steps.title: Stress the available liquidity
sop_steps.action: Apply thirty extra collection days and remove disputed invoices from assumed credit availability.
sop_steps.detail: Compare the lowest weekly cash balance with committed funds after supplier obligations and refund exposure.

sop_steps.title: Authorize only funded delivery starts
sop_steps.action: Schedule new engagements only when available cash and executable financing cover the stressed weekly deficit.
sop_steps.detail: If funding fails, reduce concurrent starts, obtain permitted advances, or renegotiate milestone and supplier payment intervals.

sections.heading: 4. Stress revenue, replacement labor, and acquisition before expanding capacity
paragraphs: Run sensitivities against recognized fees, not the government contract's headline value. A 10% reduction in recognized revenue with annual costs held fixed reduces owner profit to $6,000 Conservative, $70,000 Base, and $200,000 Scaled. The resulting margins are approximately 5.56%, 13.89%, and 22.22%. Separately, a 10% increase in delivery labor reduces profit to $12,600, $100,800, and $258,000. Combining both shocks leaves only $600, $44,800, and $158,000 before any additional financing expense. These are deliberately blunt fixed-cost tests, appropriate when employees, subscriptions, and subcontractor minimums cannot be removed immediately. Do not claim that all costs automatically decline with lost awards. An increase in contractual fee credits equal to two percentage points of gross billings costs another $2,520, $11,600, or $20,800, respectively; use the gross-billings denominator rather than recognized revenue for that calculation. Keep each stress separate unless explicitly constructing a combined scenario. A credit-loss shock belongs below recognized revenue, while a scope credit changes the transaction price above it. This separation preserves a useful diagnosis: weak scope control, weak collections, and weak labor pricing require different corrective actions.

Customer acquisition deserves its own loss funnel. With a hypothetical 25% conversion from fully qualified proposals to paying customers, six, fourteen, and twenty customers require twenty-four, fifty-six, and eighty proposals. Acquisition budgets therefore support average proposal costs of $500, $1,000, and $1,000. Those costs include screening, estimating, document preparation, and unsuccessful submissions; they exclude delivery already charged to contracted customers. If conversion falls to 20% while proposal counts and spend remain fixed, expected customer counts fall to 4.8, 11.2, and sixteen, and expected acquisition cost per customer rises to $2,500, $5,000, and $5,000. Fractional customers describe an expected-value planning model, not actual engagements. Protect the funnel by checking amendment history, incumbent advantages, mandatory site visits, wage determinations, and realistic subcontractor availability before paying for a proposal. SAM.gov alerts and bid calendars reduce monitoring effort but do not establish eligibility or commercial viability. For covered federal service work, the Service Contract Labor Standards statute and applicable wage determination can invalidate a cheap labor quote. Rebid with verified rates or decline; automation cannot repair a spread built on unpaid benefits or unavailable personnel.

Translate these tests into operating limits rather than decorative charts. Give each engagement a maximum funded exposure, a minimum post-delivery contribution, and a documented replacement-provider budget. Under the Base waterfall, $560,000 of fees less $252,000 delivery labor leaves $308,000 before acquisition; that pool must still cover $182,000 of acquisition and other overhead to produce $126,000 owner profit. A single $15,000 replacement expense therefore consumes approximately 11.9% of annual Base owner profit even though it is only 2.7% of revenue. Secure backup janitorial crews, alternate courier capacity, or replacement linguists before the service failure, with documented prices and applicable qualifications. Review cohort credits monthly against actual root causes and revise future quotes without retroactively disguising failed jobs. For an early-stage desk, the stated six-to-eighteen-month time to first deal also requires a separate pre-revenue runway; mature annual margins do not fund months before the first collection. Expand only when the existing book demonstrates repeatable acceptance, collectible invoices, and funded replacement capacity. When those conditions fail, narrow the scope to paid bid-desk deliverables, reduce concurrent launches, or pursue permitted unrestricted work instead of borrowing to preserve an unsupported headline spread.

chapters.pull_quote: A management spread is real only after earned fees cover failed bids, replacement labor, and the cash gap before collection.
action_checklist: Build an engagement-level revenue bridge separating underlying contract value, earned desk fees, scope credits, valid receivables, and collected cash.
Reconcile the three annual scenarios to $120,000, $560,000, and $1,000,000 revenue and $18,000, $126,000, and $300,000 owner profit.
Verify prime-sub structure, contingent-fee terms, similarly situated supplier status where relevant, and the actual management work supporting every spread.
Create a thirteen-week cash forecast with separate acceptance holds, invoice DSO, supplier due dates, available advances, and executable credit.
Stress every cohort for 10% lower fees, 10% higher delivery labor, thirty extra collection days, and a priced replacement-provider event.
Limit concurrent starts to funded capacity and validate employee compensation, contractor availability, wage determinations, and pre-revenue runway before hiring.

statutory_citations.title: FAR 52.215-23 — Limitations on Pass-Through Charges
statutory_citations.relevance: Supports examination of substantive added value and excessive pass-through charges where the clause applies to the contracting structure.

statutory_citations.title: 41 U.S.C. 2102 — Prohibitions on disclosing and obtaining procurement information
statutory_citations.relevance: Restricts access to specified contractor bid, proposal, and source-selection information; public opportunity monitoring does not authorize protected disclosures.

statutory_citations.title: 41 U.S.C. 8702 — Prohibition on kickbacks
statutory_citations.relevance: Prohibits covered kickbacks and prevents acquisition budgets or supplier commissions from being used to purchase favorable contract treatment.

statutory_citations.title: 31 U.S.C. 3903 — Regulations governing prompt payment
statutory_citations.relevance: Provides the statutory framework for federal payment timing, proper invoices, and acceptance procedures rather than an assumed universal subcontract DSO.

statutory_citations.title: FAR 52.232-40 — Providing Accelerated Payments to Small Business Subcontractors
statutory_citations.relevance: Addresses acceleration of payments under the clause's conditions and explains why subcontract cash forecasts must still use actual contractual obligations.

statutory_citations.title: 41 U.S.C. 6703 — Required contract terms for covered service contracts
statutory_citations.relevance: Requires specified wage and fringe-benefit provisions for covered federal service contracts, affecting fulfillment quotes and replacement labor economics.

statutory_citations.title: 31 U.S.C. 3727 — Assignments of claims
statutory_citations.relevance: Requires transaction-specific review before relying on assignment of claims against the United States as a receivables-financing mechanism.

chapters.question_prompt: How do you allocate startup capital ($20,000–$90,000 USD) and configure a lean, low-opex ($5,000–$25,000 USD/mo) production stack without wasting cash on bloated overhead?
chapters.title: Startup Capital, Lean Infrastructure & Pre-Flight Stack
chapters.subtitle: Reserve-First Bid Desks, SAM.gov Intelligence, Lawful Teaming, and FAR-Aware Production Controls
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #4, Government Contract Brokering, ranks #27 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Build a procurement service, not a speculative inventory book: reserve 60% of startup capital, buy delivery capacity against signed work, and separate recurring overhead from project costs. This chapter maps seven operating plays: solicitation intelligence, bid-calendar management, proposal production, prime/sub teaming, supplier verification, invoice administration, and transferable tax-credit brokerage. The first six are chapter operating applications; the seventh carries the supplied catalog identifier. Annual owner profit remains $18,000 Conservative, $126,000 Base, and $300,000 Scaled. A twelve-layer stack, explicit cash runway, entity and insurance controls, and evidence-based launch checks prevent award uncertainty, slow collections, and supplier failure from consuming the business before repeatable service revenue arrives.

sections.heading: 1. Protect the reserve before funding the first bid desk
paragraphs: Start with the cash calendar, not the software catalog. Government Contract Brokering has a six-to-eighteen-month first-deal horizon, so allocate 60% of each startup package to working capital before signing annual contracts. At $25,000, that means $15,000 reserved and $10,000 available for setup; at $75,000, reserve $45,000; at $150,000, reserve $90,000. Keep the reserve in a business deposit account separate from operating disbursements, with weekly reconciliation and an explicit minimum balance. At $5,000 monthly cash burn, those reserves cover three, nine, and eighteen months; at $25,000, they cover only 0.6, 1.8, and 3.6 months. These calculations exclude receipts and assume the setup allocation has already been spent. The smallest package therefore cannot independently finance the stated sales cycle. Its viable entry is a founder-led desk with prepaid private-client research assignments, staged setup purchases, or additional committed funding. Do not solve that mismatch by describing an unsigned award as cash. Publish a thirteen-week forecast showing beginning cash, collectible invoices, contractor commitments, insurance installments, and ending reserve. Extend the forecast monthly through eighteen months, including the collection lag after the first signed engagement.

Treat the $5,000–$25,000 monthly operating range as a controlled overhead envelope, not proof that every scorecard case fits inside it. A lean $5,000 planning envelope can allocate $300 to software and communications, $800 to insurance and professional-support accruals, $2,200 to limited paid delivery capacity, $700 to targeted prospecting, and $1,000 to administration and contingency. Contractor hours must fit the actual rate card; $2,200 buys forty hours at $55, not a full proposal department. Larger assignments require separately priced delivery budgets and collection terms. The canonical annual expense residuals are $102,000 Conservative, $434,000 Base, and $700,000 Scaled, obtained by subtracting owner profit from recognized service revenue. Their monthly equivalents are $8,500, about $36,167, and about $58,333. Therefore, Base and Scaled require delivery and other costs outside the recurring overhead envelope; calling that envelope total business expense would break the model. The specified teams remain 2 FT + 3 C, 2 FT + 3 C, and 3 FT + 4 C. Those labels do not establish affordable market salaries. Validate paid hours, benefits, founder compensation treatment, and contractor utilization before using any scenario as a hiring authorization.

Release setup money in evidence-backed increments. Entity formation, contract review, banking, insurance placement, and secure document handling precede paid intelligence subscriptions. A federal prospect does not justify leasing an office, hiring a salaried capture executive, or buying warehouse stock. The allocation matrix contains spending ceilings rather than instructions to exhaust each category. Unused amounts return to the reserve, and no contingency dollar supports a speculative supplier deposit. For direct private-client services, negotiate a defined onboarding deliverable and an initial payment where commercially acceptable; federal contract payment terms are controlled by the actual award and applicable clauses. Never import private-client deposit assumptions into an agency purchase order. Establish separate accounts receivable aging for commercial retainers, prime-contractor subcontract invoices, and direct government invoices because each has different acceptance evidence and dispute routes. A $12,000 service invoice delayed sixty days ties up $12,000 of liquidity even when accounting profit looks healthy. Before increasing fixed overhead, require signed scope, measurable delivery capacity, and cash coverage through a delayed-payment scenario. If the reserve falls below the next eight weeks of committed disbursements, stop optional subscriptions and decline bids requiring unfunded deposits or irreversible third-party commitments.

sections.heading: 2. Configure twelve production layers without buying twelve subscriptions
paragraphs: The twelve-layer matrix is a procurement worksheet, not a live vendor quotation. Dollar figures are explicit planning assumptions for the named tiers, in United States dollars before tax; paid annual-billing tiers show monthly equivalents and must be checked at checkout. Product packaging, seat minimums, and included capabilities can change. Start with the free layers and purchase paid seats only for people who produce or control deliverables. The illustrated minimum paid stack is two Google Workspace Business Starter seats at $7 each, two Bitwarden Teams seats at $4 each, one QuickBooks Simple Start subscription budgeted at $38, and one DocuSign Personal subscription budgeted at $10: $70 monthly equivalent. That is a software subtotal, not the firm's total infrastructure cost. It excludes hardware, domains, telephone service, tax, insurance, paid backup, and any annual prepayment. DocuSign's planned five-envelope monthly allowance must fit actual signature volume; replace it with an acceptable client signature workflow before paying for excess capacity. Free Airtable, Trello, and HubSpot layers can overlap, so activate only the interfaces that reduce handoffs. A spreadsheet with one accountable owner beats three unmaintained databases with conflicting opportunity deadlines.

For the solicitation-intelligence play, combine SAM.gov saved searches with municipal Bonfire and OpenGov Procurement notices. Record agency, notice identifier, amendment sequence, due time with time zone, NAICS code, set-aside status, and source link. An alert is a lead, not an authoritative deadline; the current solicitation and amendments control. Price an illustrative private-client monitoring package at $500 monthly for eight curated briefs. Two analyst hours at $60 plus $20 of allocated tools leave $360 before selling, management, and other expenses. If fewer than eight relevant opportunities exist, report that fact rather than padding the feed. For bid-calendar management, a $750 monthly service with three hours at $60 and $30 allocated tooling leaves $540 before other costs. Its fallback is a versioned spreadsheet and dual calendar reminders, not blind reliance on an API. For proposal production, a $4,000 fixed-scope package using thirty hours at $70 and $200 of outside review leaves $1,700 before overhead. Scope excludes technical claims the client cannot substantiate. Amendment-driven rewrites receive a written change order; a missing technical owner triggers a no-bid recommendation rather than fabricated qualifications.

Design security around the data actually authorized for the desk. Enforce multifactor authentication, individual accounts, encrypted disks, device updates, and role-limited client folders before importing the first proposal. Do not place credentials, banking instructions, personnel records, or restricted technical material in public Trello boards or shared chatbot workspaces. The starter stack is not an assertion that it meets Controlled Unclassified Information requirements. If a contract introduces FAR 52.204-21, DFARS 252.204-7012, or other security obligations, identify the covered information and required environment before accepting it. Decline receipt until the applicable controls and contractual responsibilities are implemented. Maintain a register for systems of record: HubSpot owns client contacts, the opportunity ledger owns deadlines, Drive owns approved working documents, and the accounting system owns invoices. Export those records weekly to access-controlled storage and test restoration quarterly; an export is useful only if relationships and attachments survive. Use SAM.gov APIs within published access conditions and rate limits, retaining source timestamps. Scripts may suggest classifications or checklist entries, but a named reviewer verifies eligibility, mandatory forms, pricing units, and submission acknowledgments. Automation should remove rekeying, never transfer responsibility for a missed amendment to software.

callout.title: Buy evidence quality before buying more alerts
callout.body: Experienced bid desks reduce avoidable rework by controlling amendments, access, and scope before expanding their tool budget.
items: Store the original notice, each amendment, and the retrieval timestamp together; never let a rewritten summary replace the controlling solicitation.
Run a two-week comparison of paid intelligence against SAM.gov and agency portals; cancel when the paid feed adds no qualified, timely opportunities.
Ask municipal procurement staff which portal issues the controlling addenda, then document that answer in the opportunity record.
Price proposal revisions by the changed requirement and affected pages; do not sell unlimited amendment handling inside a small fixed fee.

sections.heading: 3. Establish lawful service boundaries, banking controls, and seven play economics
paragraphs: Form the operating entity in the jurisdiction where it actually conducts business, obtain its EIN, document ownership, and open a business account under the same legal identity used on contracts and invoices. Confirm current federal and state reporting duties rather than copying an old formation checklist. SAM.gov registration and a Unique Entity ID are free; pursue the registration needed for the firm's actual federal role without charging clients a fictitious government registration fee. A service provider advising bidders is not automatically the prime contractor. Written engagements must identify who submits, who signs certifications, who performs, and who gets paid. Review FAR Subpart 3.4 and FAR 52.203-5 before any compensation tied to winning a federal contract; a broker label does not establish a bona fide agency exception. Protect nonpublic procurement information under 41 U.S.C. chapter 21, and prohibit improper payments under 41 U.S.C. chapter 87. Maintain general liability, professional liability, cyber coverage, and required workers' compensation according to actual exposures and contract terms. Verify exclusions, deductibles, defense-cost treatment, and subcontractor coverage with the carrier. A certificate evidences coverage information; it does not rewrite the policy or confer protection that an exclusion removes.

The next three operating plays monetize documented work rather than access to an award decision. Prime/sub teaming coordination can carry a $2,500 fixed diligence fee: twenty hours at $75 plus $250 of document review leaves $750 before overhead. If the contemplated arrangement depends on unperformed work, undisclosed commissions, or prohibited pass-through economics, stop structuring it and return only the contracted diligence findings. For covered set-asides, examine 13 CFR 125.6 and the applicable FAR 52.219-14 clause; the calculation depends on contract category and treatment of similarly situated entities. Supplier verification can charge $900 for a defined evidence packet: eight hours at $65 plus $80 of verification expense leaves $300 before overhead. Verify capacity, relevant registrations, exclusion status, quoted lead times, and references; otherwise narrow the finding rather than issue an unsupported endorsement. Invoice administration can charge $600 monthly for twenty documented invoices: four hours at $60 plus $20 allocated tools leaves $340 before overhead. Require acceptance records and submission receipts; disputed invoices escalate to the contracting parties. These examples, together with the three preceding plays, are chapter-level operating applications, not additional supplied catalog identifiers. Their contribution calculations are illustrative and must not be added to canonical revenue.

The seventh mapped play is transferable_tax_credit_brokerage_syndication, a separate specialist workflow rather than a government-award commission. Originate leads from public DOE and EPA project datasets, grid-operator interconnection queues, state film offices, and historic-preservation registries using permitted access methods. DOE and EPA records are not universal interconnection queues, and a project listing proves neither credit ownership nor transferability. For $1,000,000 of credit face value, the supplied $0.82–$0.88 seller range implies $820,000–$880,000, while $0.92–$0.96 buyer pricing implies $920,000–$960,000. The apparent $40,000–$140,000 spread is not automatically broker revenue. IRC 6418 generally bars a transferee from transferring the purchased credit again; structure an eligible producer-to-taxpayer transfer, not an intermediary resale. An illustrative separately agreed 1.5% fee on $940,000 consideration produces $14,100 service revenue. Buyer cash funds simultaneous escrow disbursements, with no broker inventory or bridge advance. Bind non-cancelable tax-credit insurance acceptable to the parties and verify exclusions and cancellation rights; if unavailable, decline the transaction under this play's required fallback. Georgia, Louisiana, historic, and brownfield programs require separate transfer analysis. Screen individual buyers for passive-activity limits, and obtain specialist review of eligibility, registration, recapture allocation, and transfer documentation.
